1:
The fleeing wicked man is drawn from within. Gill collects the biblical instances of terror without an object — the first murderer, the captain who took mountain shadows for an army, the man chased by a shaken leaf. Henry supplies the domestic version: guilt makes a man a terror to himself, so that he behaves like a debtor in hiding who takes every passer-by for a bailiff, and one who has made God his enemy must see the whole creation at war with him. Sin makes men cowards, he concludes, and asks what they will do when God himself pursues. Clarke agrees that however bold the wicked appear they carry dreary apprehensions about both worlds, and notes an old English rendering that calls the fugitive unpitious, since pity once meant piety. Delitzsch spends his note on accents and grammar, defending the received division.

Where the second verse blames a nation's instability on its sin, they differ on the mechanism. Gill supplies both readings of many princes: rivals reigning at once, as when thirty tyrants rose together at Athens, or a rapid succession cut short by deposition or death, with new laws and fresh taxes at every turn. Henry keeps to the moral: a people crumbled into factions devouring one another. Clarke offers political theory: nations cannot be judged as nations in another world, so God judges them in this one, and where people believe the constitution favours them they leave the ruler alone as guardian of their privileges. Ellicott contrasts the northern kingdom's assassinations with the regular Davidic succession, and takes the second clause to promise a settled condition rather than length of days.

The poor oppressor drew out exegetes and moralists alike. Delitzsch reports an alternative construing that makes the verse a proportion — the tyrant is to his victims what a flood is to a people it starves — and rejects it, since two of the four terms then collapse together and the comparison explains a thing by itself; the sweeping rain is rain without rain's benefit. Gill and Ellicott read the oppressor as a man risen from poverty, of whom compassion might have been expected and who grows harder for having suffered. Henry says it in proverbs: the hungry leech and the dry sponge suck most, and a beggar set on horseback rides without mercy — whence his rule that men in debt should not be given places of trust. Clarke finds the parable of the two debtors an exact illustration, and adds that eastern rains of this kind carry off flocks, crops and houses. Wesley calls the man the worst of all oppressors.

Praise and reproof divide the next verse. Gill notices how commendation works, one covetous man calling another's greed good husbandry, one proud man calling another's disdain a sense of rank; Henry adds that nothing serves the devil's kingdom so well as keeping vice in reputation, and that whoever praises the wicked has abandoned the law condemning them. Delitzsch and Wesley take the answering clause as anger passing into action, a zeal that cannot keep silent, and Ellicott finds its pattern in a Lord who bore insults unmoved and grew angry only at wrongdoing. On understanding, Delitzsch holds that a man who makes wickedness his element loses the moral concepts themselves, while one whose end is God finds there the knowledge of what is right in any situation — a potential and relative knowledge, he cautions, not omniscience. Henry runs the causation both ways, lust darkening the mind and the darkened mind feeding the lust. The closing comparison turns for Delitzsch and Ellicott on a phrase meaning double-going: not a man who strays from the road but one who walks an evil way while appearing to walk a good one. Henry answers the world's incredulity with the statesman who told a rich man that wealth hurt him more than poverty hurt the poor.
7:
Delitzsch takes the law of the seventh verse to include a father's instruction; the companions waste means and health together, and the verb of shaming covers both the disgrace the son inflicts and the disgrace others heap on his household. Henry works that point hardest: bad company does not merely grieve parents but discredits them, as if they had failed in their duty. Gill turns the keeping inward: a delight in the law after the inward man, service rendered from love, a reward in obedience though never for it.

Usury draws the sharpest language in the chapter. Gill assembles the etymologies — the Hebrew word means biting, the Greeks called interest a birth because money breeds money, the Latin term resembles their word for offspring — and notes that what swells one estate devours another. Delitzsch notes that the two terms were distinguished in the law as interest in money and interest in kind, and that a marginal reading seems meant to soften the doubling. On the outcome all agree, Henry most fully: ill-gotten wealth does not last, and providence transfers it into hands that will use it mercifully, so that one act punishes cruelty and rewards charity, as the hidden pound went to the servant who had ten — a comparison Ellicott makes too. Clarke abandons exposition and wishes such lenders named at every market cross and shipped to the far side of the world.

The stopped ear and the abominable prayer produce agreement. Delitzsch observes that what is condemned is not such a man's wickedness only but his apparent goodness, since he is not the person his prayer represents and does not truly want what he asks. Henry frames it as a broken conversation — God speaks by his word, we answer by prayer — and notes that even prayer, a moral duty and not a ceremonial one, offends when the word is refused; a man who will not hear when God calls is justly unheard. Clarke identifies the motive: many avoid whatever might enlighten them, believing ignorance will excuse them, and he answers that the servant who might have known his master's will fares no better than the one who knew.

Seducers fare worse. Delitzsch has the misleader fall into the destruction he prepared, and points out that calling his victims upright aggravates the crime, since they deserved better; Gill and Henry both add that the attempt cannot finally succeed against the elect, so the man loses his object and keeps his punishment. Clarke sees the purpose: contempt poured on religion by a convert's fall. On the rich man's self-estimate Delitzsch is exact: he seems wise in his own eyes, but a poor man of understanding gets to the bottom of him, probably while being used as an instrument, wisdom being a gift that does not follow property. Henry supplies the social detail — the purse-proud man expects every sheaf to bow to his, and is confirmed by flatterers who eat at his table — and adds that the poor man, lacking any other route to a reputation, acquires understanding and exposes him.

The last verse turns on one Hebrew word. Ellicott reports that what the English renders hidden means literally sought for: good men hide from fear and must be hunted out. Delitzsch reads the clause as the people being searched, and glosses the opposite half through an Arabic idiom for a festival day, so that the glory of the first line is the putting on of holiday clothes. Henry and Wesley take the verse politically: prosperity means good men are advanced and hold office, and the rise of the wicked means they withdraw into obscure places, until it can look, as it did to Elijah, as though none were left. Gill adds the free exercise of religion to the blessings; Clarke dates both halves from English history, one reign against the reign that followed.
13:
On concealing sin the group is nearly unanimous; the interest is in the qualifications. Gill guards the maxim: God may cover a man's transgressions, and it is the glory of his grace to do so; forbidden is covering one's own. Covering means denying when charged, justifying, extenuating, or shifting the blame to whoever drew him in, as the first man did. Delitzsch insists the promise attaches to both halves of the clause, since remission does not follow confession where new obedience is absent, and leaves the unconfessed man under a secret ban. Henry says it in images — the concealed distemper that cannot be cured, the bird of the air that carries the voice — and adds that when we set sin before our face God casts it behind him. Ellicott alone limits the mercy: the penitent is fully forgiven, yet may bear the temporal penalty still, and will find the next temptation harder for having yielded.

The happy fear divides on its object. Delitzsch reports that one Jewish commentator made God the thing feared, and prefers sin, since the pious man fears God and dreads evil at once; the verb means the watch kept against harm reaching one's soul. Gill excludes the servile fear of wrath that has torment in it, and settles on a filial reverence arising from a sense of God's goodness. Ellicott makes it self-distrust that sends a man for aid. Henry states the paradox: most think those happy who never fear, whereas the blessed man is jealous of himself and expects trouble, so it never surprises. Against him stands the hardened man, steeling himself, in Delitzsch's account, against God's word and against all who care for his soul.

The lion and the bear bring out the naturalists. Gill has the lion roaring for want of food, and derives the bear's name from its hungry growl. Delitzsch defines the ranging bear as one driven about by extreme hunger, and notes that the Greek version made it a wolf. He and Ellicott stress that the people are poor in the sense of defenceless, stripped by war and unable to resist, which makes the tyrant a double terror. Henry, aware that scripture forbids speaking evil of a ruler, notes that scripture itself supplied these terms, and that such a man belongs among beasts of prey rather than creatures whose glory is reason.

The prince who lacks understanding is grammatically contested. Older interpreters made it a statement: a ruler short of sense is long on oppression. Delitzsch objects that the conjunction will not carry it, and reads an address instead, a warning called out to the prince. On the substance everyone joins him. Henry names the two causes of misgovernment as love of money and failure to calculate, and holds tyrants the greatest fools alive, safer as they would be in their subjects' affections than in their fortifications. Clarke observes that a weak prince gathers wicked ministers, preferring flatterers, and makes the mildness of a government the measure of a king's intellect. Ellicott adds the economic version: such a man kills the goose that laid the golden eggs.

The last verse turns on whether its subject acts or suffers. The English has a man doing violence to blood; Delitzsch argues at length that the Hebrew form cannot mean oppressing, only oppressed, and renders a man burdened with the guilt of blood, which is Ellicott's reading too. Gill offers the same in a psychological key, a murderer tortured in his own conscience, and reports an old observation about an undersized letter in the word for man, read as marking one red with blood. On the second clause all agree. Henry has the murderer haunted like the first fugitive, and warns that whoever helps him off shares the guilt of blood; Clarke says none should shelter him, the law having its claim; Wesley, that none should so much as wish to.
18:
Two words carry the eighteenth verse. The perverse man carries the same double-way phrase used earlier, and the adverb of his fall means not sometime but at once — falling wholly, Delitzsch glosses, so that no second blow is needed, a sense Schultens matched with Virgil's line about a man who bit the ground once and died. Clarke says it in four words: he falls without resource. Ellicott adds that it comes unannounced. Henry draws out why that matters: such a man is least safe when he feels safest, with no time to guard against ruin or prepare for it. Integrity gives holy security in the worst of times, and upright men may be injured but cannot be hurt. Gill will not have walking uprightly earn the salvation: it describes who is saved, grace being the moving cause and Christ the procuring.

Tillage and faithfulness go together. Delitzsch notes the symmetry of the nineteenth verse, one verb of satisfaction governing bread and poverty alike, and Henry presses the irony: the idler takes courses leading so directly to want that he seems to court it. On the faithful man Delitzsch takes the Hebrew plural to mark a rectitude unbroken and visible on every side, the blessings covering what God gives and what men speak. Gill spells out the moral version — true to his work, keeping promises, honouring contracts — and adds that such a man is usually charitable, abounding in blessings received and given. Henry makes usefulness the reward of faithfulness, and is careful with the other clause: the text does not say the man in haste to be rich cannot be innocent, only that he probably will not.

Partiality produces a disagreement over scale. Delitzsch thinks it too low a conception to read the morsel of bread as the bribe's size; the point is that even a trifle can raise a liking or a grudge and bend the will from strict rectitude, and he cites the Roman tribune hirable with a scrap of bread to speak or keep silent. Henry takes the opposite road and makes the smallness the point: men who broke the bonds of equity for a noble present end by selling judgment for a crust, preferring small game to sitting out. Wesley agrees that habit cheapens the price. Gill widens the fault beyond the courts to assemblies that distinguish rich from poor, and Ellicott adds that servility degrades as its price falls.

The man in a hurry to be rich returns with an evil eye. Delitzsch identifies it as envy joined to covetousness, and grants that such a man may merely eat himself with ill-humour, though as a rule envy sets him striving to match the prosperity he resents — a zeal from an impure motive, blind to the fact that he sinks rather than rises, since discontent forfeits even what God assigned. Henry says the same from within: he grieves at those who have more and grudges what he must spend, never at ease, and the riches he made wings for will make wings to fly from him. Ellicott and Wesley make the evil eye ungenerous as well as jealous.

The last verse is textually vexed, and the argument turns on one small word. Gill follows the accents in attaching it to the first clause, so the reproof is given after God's directions, or after Solomon's example, as the Targum takes it. Delitzsch rejects that — a teacher naming himself so would be pointless — with the Talmudic reference to God and the emendations others propose, the form being unlikely to occur just once if it existed. His own rendering gives the phrase to the man rebuked, one going backwards; Ellicott records that and the ordinary sense both. Henry ignores the philology and supplies the picture: a patient who cries out at the surgeon probing his wound and pays him gladly once it is healed.
24:
Robbing a parent is worse than ordinary theft for the excuse attached. Delitzsch defines the destroyer as one who ruins from appetite rather than revenge, and notes the son's excuse that it will all be his eventually. Ellicott gives the same reasoning, and answers that a quiet deed is no better than open violence. Clarke puts it sharply: to the child, a parent's property is as much another's as a stranger's, so such a son adds ingratitude and cruelty to robbery. Henry catalogues the methods — force, stealth, wheedling, threats, wasting the estate, leaving debts for the parents to settle — then the pleas: it will be ours shortly, they can spare it, a young gentleman cannot live on his allowance. What crime, he asks, will such a son scruple at?

The proud heart is set against the trusting, and that against the self-trusting. Gill reads the enlarged heart as either covetousness, quarrelling through lawsuits and unpaid debts, or pride that cannot bear contradiction. Delitzsch works the verb, whose root means to grind, and pauses over an idiom: we would call such a man a hot-head, but the biblical writers never locate mental events in the head. He reports the Greek reading, that the patient man stifles a quarrel before it breaks out, and judges both true — he settles strife he is drawn into and prevents what would otherwise begin. Henry balances the halves as leanness against fatness: the quarrelsome make themselves uneasy, while the man who commits his cause to God saves what others spend on pride, none living so pleasantly as those who live by faith.

On trusting one's own heart Delitzsch notices that the proverb was placed here by catchword, taking up the trust of the verse before, and rejects reading the heart as courage, the word alone never meaning that. What is attacked, he says, is a false subjectivity: the heart manufactures thoughts of which scripture says nothing good, while wisdom comes from above and is knowledge of what is objectively true. Gill presses past the obvious target: not the openly self-righteous only but a good man relying on his own sincerity is deceived, as one apostle was. Henry adds that the heart a man trusts has already deceived him often, and Wesley draws the rule: walking wisely means distrusting one's judgment and seeking counsel from others and God. Clarke states it in a line: that heart will infallibly deceive him.

Almsgiving draws the chapter's most attractive comments. Henry advises the man with little to give out of his little, since that preserves it, as the widow who baked the prophet his cake first kept her meal; what we gave, he says, we have. He notices too the gesture of the other clause, a man covering his eyes lest the sight reach his heart, and calls that condition woeful, the word of God and the prayers of the poor both against him. Delitzsch makes the accounting explicit: the giver wants nothing because the blessing reimburses him, while the man who veils his eyes grows rich in curses instead, which, being deserved, turn by requital into misfortunes. Gill adds that the giver never misses it, and records an older reading applying the verse to a teacher withholding no doctrine from his pupil.

The closing verse repeats the twelfth; the fresh question is what increase means. Delitzsch declines the reading that has the righteous emerge into public view, preferring growth: they multiply as plants do once the caterpillars are dealt with. Henry keeps to the political sense: the wise decline office, the rich get out of the way lest they be squeezed, good men abscond in despair; when the wicked fall, better men take their room, which is why rulers should attend to the education of the young. Gill and Wesley describe the hiding briefly, adding that some hide from shame at what they would otherwise see.
